s1-0.ref: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy (Upper Limb); Gray's Anatomy
w: Correct. The axillary nerve winds round the surgical neck, supplies deltoid and teres minor, and gives the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (the 'badge' area).
Suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus. Injury weakens the first 15° of abduction and lateral rotation, and causes no skin loss over the deltoid.
Radial nerve is injured in the spiral groove (midshaft fracture), causing wrist drop. Shoulder abduction is spared.
Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion and supination, with sensory loss on the lateral forearm, not over the deltoid.
steps: Fracture site given: surgical neck of humerus.
Ask which nerve hugs that site: the axillary nerve.
Check motor: deltoid paralysed, so abduction stops after supraspinatus starts it.
Check sensory: lower deltoid skin = upper lateral cutaneous nerve of arm, a branch of axillary. Diagnosis confirmed.
s1-0.mn: Fracture-nerve pairs, top to bottom of the humerus: 'ARMU' = Axillary, Radial, Median, Ulnar.

s1-1.ref: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy (Upper Limb); Gray's Anatomy
w: Correct. A wrist-level ulnar injury spares FDP to the ring and little fingers, so their distal joints flex more and the claw looks worse.
Froment sign tests adductor pollicis (ulnar): the patient flexes the thumb IP joint with FPL when gripping paper.
Wartenberg sign is persistent abduction of the little finger from weak palmar interossei. It is a sign, not the paradox.
Benediction attitude is seen when the median nerve is injured above the elbow and the patient tries to make a fist.
steps: Clawing = MCP hyperextension + IP flexion of the ring and little fingers.
IP flexion needs a working FDP (medial half = ulnar nerve in the forearm).
A wrist lesion keeps FDP working, so flexion is stronger and the claw more obvious.
A higher lesion paralyses FDP too, so the claw is milder: this is the paradox.

w: Correct. The SA nodal artery arises from the RCA in about 60% of people.
LAD supplies the anterior septum and anterior LV wall. It is not the usual origin of the SA nodal artery.
The circumflex gives the SA nodal artery in the remaining ~40%, so it is not the most common origin.
The posterior interventricular artery supplies the posterior septum and, in right dominance, comes from the RCA. It does not give the SA nodal artery.
steps: Recall the SA nodal artery runs up to the crista terminalis area.
Most often it is a branch of the RCA.
Contrast with the AV nodal artery, which follows dominance.
Link: RCA occlusion (inferior MI) causes sinus bradycardia or AV block.

s1-3.ref: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (neuro-ophthalmology); Vishram Singh Neuroanatomy
w: Correct. Right MLF lesion: the right eye cannot adduct on left gaze, and the abducting left eye shows nystagmus. Convergence is preserved.
An abducens nucleus lesion causes ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy (both eyes cannot look to that side), not isolated failure of adduction.
An oculomotor nerve palsy would also impair convergence, cause ptosis and a 'down and out' eye, and often a dilated pupil.
A PPRF lesion causes conjugate gaze palsy to the same side, again affecting both eyes.

k: Named for side that fails to adduct

steps: Abnormal eye: the right eye fails to adduct.
Adduction works on convergence, so the III nerve and medial rectus are fine.
The lesion must be in the pathway linking the left VI nucleus to the right III nucleus: the right MLF.
Young woman + INO = think multiple sclerosis.
s1-3.mn: 'MLF = MS Loves Fasciculus': bilateral INO in a young adult is MS until proven otherwise.

s1-4.ref: Dhingra's Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat; Gray's Anatomy
w: Correct. Cricothyroid is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
Posterior cricoarytenoid (the only abductor) is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Lateral cricoarytenoid (adductor) is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Thyroarytenoid (relaxes cords) is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
steps: Remember the rule: the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except one.
The exception is cricothyroid, on the outside of the larynx.
Its nerve is the external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
Clinical link: injury in thyroidectomy gives voice fatigue and loss of high pitch.
s1-4.mn: 'Cricothyroid is the outsider': on the outside, with the outside (external) nerve.

s1-5.ref: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy (Abdomen); Gray's Anatomy
w: Correct. The free border of the lesser omentum, containing the portal triad, lies in front of the foramen.
The IVC forms the posterior boundary.
The caudate process of the liver forms the superior boundary.
The first part of the duodenum forms the inferior boundary.
steps: The foramen connects the greater sac to the lesser sac.
Put a finger in it: in front is the hepatoduodenal ligament.
Behind is the IVC, above the caudate process, below the duodenum.
Surgical use: the Pringle manoeuvre compresses the anterior boundary.
s1-5.mn: Hepatoduodenal ligament contents, right to left: 'DAVe' = Duct (CBD) right, Artery left, Vein behind.

s1-6.ref: Langman's Medical Embryology; Inderbir Singh's Human Embryology
w: Correct. The second arch (Reichert cartilage) forms the stapes, styloid process and lesser horn of the hyoid.
The first arch (Meckel cartilage) forms the malleus and incus, not the stapes.
The third arch forms the greater horn and lower body of the hyoid.
The fourth arch forms laryngeal cartilages (thyroid), not ear ossicles.

r: Stapes, styloid, lesser horn of hyoid

steps: Ear ossicles come from the first two arches.
Malleus and incus: first arch.
Stapes: second arch (a stapes 'S' for second).
Match the nerve: the 2nd arch nerve is the facial nerve, which also supplies stapedius.
s1-6.mn: 'S for Stapes, S for Second (and Styloid).'

s1-7.ref: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy (Lower Limb); Gray's Anatomy
w: Correct. Standing on the right leg, the right gluteus medius and minimus (superior gluteal nerve) must hold the pelvis level. When they are weak, the left side drops.
The left superior gluteal nerve would cause a drop on the right when standing on the left leg.
The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus. Its loss affects rising from sitting and climbing stairs, not pelvic tilt.
The femoral nerve supplies quadriceps (knee extension), which does not stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance.
steps: Identify the stance leg: right.
Hip abductors of the stance leg keep the opposite side of the pelvis up.
If the left side drops, the right abductors are weak.
The right hip abductors are supplied by the right superior gluteal nerve.
s1-7.mn: 'The Sound Side Sags': the pelvis drops on the healthy side.

s1-8.ref: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Harrison's
w: Correct. In AV dissociation the atrium sometimes contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, giving large intermittent cannon waves.
Atrial fibrillation has no organised atrial contraction, so the 'a' wave is absent.
Tricuspid regurgitation gives large 'v' (cv) waves, not cannon 'a' waves.
Constrictive pericarditis gives a steep 'y' descent (and Kussmaul sign).
steps: 'a' = atrial contraction.
Cannon = atrium contracts against a closed valve.
This happens when atria and ventricles beat independently.
Complete heart block causes AV dissociation, so cannon waves appear.

s1-9.ref: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; West's Respiratory Physiology
w: Correct. Perfusion falls more steeply than ventilation towards the apex, so V/Q is highest there (about 3).
The base has the lowest V/Q (about 0.6) because perfusion is greatest there.
The mid-zone has an intermediate ratio.
V/Q is not uniform; gravity creates a gradient from apex to base.
steps: Both ventilation and perfusion increase towards the base.
Perfusion increases much more steeply.
So the ratio is highest where perfusion is least: the apex.
Clinical link: high apical PO2 suits reactivated TB.

s1-10.ref: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology
w: Correct. Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR.
PAH clearance measures effective renal plasma flow; it is almost completely secreted.
Creatinine is slightly secreted, so it overestimates GFR, though it is used clinically.
Urea is partly reabsorbed, so its clearance underestimates GFR.
steps: Ideal GFR marker: freely filtered, not reabsorbed, not secreted, not metabolised.
Only inulin meets all four.
Creatinine is practical but slightly secreted.
PAH is for plasma flow, not GFR.

s1-11.ref: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Lippincott Biochemistry
w: Correct. GH binds a cytokine-type receptor that activates JAK2, which phosphorylates STAT proteins.
Insulin acts through a receptor tyrosine kinase (intrinsic kinase activity), not JAK-STAT.
Glucagon acts through a Gs-coupled receptor that raises cAMP.
Aldosterone is a steroid acting on an intracellular nuclear receptor.
steps: Classify each option by receptor type.
Insulin: receptor tyrosine kinase.
Glucagon: G protein → cAMP. Aldosterone: nuclear receptor.
GH: cytokine receptor family → JAK-STAT.
s1-11.mn: JAK-STAT hormones: 'PIGEonhole' = Prolactin, Interleukins, GH, EPO.

s1-12.ref: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology
w: Correct. Na+ channel inactivation gates stay closed until the membrane repolarises, so no new spike is possible.
K+ channel opening repolarises the membrane and contributes to the relative refractory period, not the absolute.
The Na+/K+ pump maintains gradients over the long term; it does not cause refractoriness.
Chloride channels do not determine the refractory period of nerve.
steps: Voltage-gated Na+ channels have three states: closed, open and inactivated.
After opening they become inactivated and cannot reopen at once.
While most are inactivated, no stimulus can trigger a spike: the absolute refractory period.
As they recover, a stronger stimulus can fire the nerve: the relative refractory period.

s1-13.ref: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology
w: Correct. I cells in the duodenum and jejunum release CCK in response to fat and protein.
S cells release secretin (bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice).
G cells in the antrum release gastrin (acid secretion).
K cells release GIP (glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide).
steps: The letter of the cell often matches: G for gastrin, S for secretin, K for GIP.
CCK is the exception to remember: I cells.
I cells sit in the duodenum and jejunum.
Fat in the duodenum → CCK → gallbladder empties.

s1-14.ref: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology
w: Correct. CO increases haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, shifting the curve left and blocking unloading to tissues.
Increased 2,3-BPG lowers affinity and shifts the curve to the right.
Hypercapnia (and acidosis) shifts the curve right (Bohr effect).
Fever (raised temperature) shifts the curve right.
steps: Right shift = tissues get O2 more easily (exercise conditions).
CO2, acid, BPG and heat all occur in working tissue, so they shift right.
CO binds Hb and makes the other haem sites hold O2 tighter: left shift.
So CO harms twice: less O2 carried and less O2 released.
s1-14.mn: Right shift: 'CADET, face Right' = CO2, Acid, 2,3-DPG, Exercise, Temperature.

s1-15.ref: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology; Ganong
w: Correct. Sleep spindles and K-complexes define stage N2.
N1 is light sleep with theta waves and vertex sharp waves.
N3 (slow-wave sleep) shows high-amplitude delta waves.
REM shows low-voltage mixed frequency and sawtooth waves, with rapid eye movements and muscle atonia.
steps: Spindles and K-complexes are unique EEG markers.
They appear only in stage N2.
N3 is defined by delta waves instead.
Remember the parasomnias: N3 = night terrors and sleepwalking; REM = nightmares.
s1-15.mn: 'At Night, BATS Drink Blood': Beta, Alpha, Theta, Spindles/K (N2), Delta (N3), Beta-like REM.

s1-16.ref: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry; Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry
w: Correct. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke) blocks free glucose release from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Acid maltase deficiency (Pompe) causes cardiomegaly and hypotonia, not fasting hypoglycaemia with lactic acidosis.
Muscle phosphorylase deficiency (McArdle) causes exercise cramps and myoglobinuria, not liver features.
Debranching enzyme deficiency (Cori) causes milder hypoglycaemia with normal lactate, because gluconeogenesis still works.
steps: Fasting hypoglycaemia + hepatomegaly = a liver GSD.
Add lactic acidosis, urate and lipids: the block is at the very last step.
The last step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis is glucose-6-phosphatase.
So the diagnosis is von Gierke disease.
s1-16.mn: GSD names in order: 'Very Poor Carbohydrate Metabolism' = Von Gierke, Pompe, Cori, McArdle (I, II, III, V).

w: Correct. HMG-CoA reductase (HMG-CoA → mevalonate) is the regulated, committed step and the statin target.
HMG-CoA synthase forms HMG-CoA; it is not rate-limiting for cholesterol.
Squalene epoxidase is a later step and is not the main regulatory point.
Mevalonate kinase acts after the committed step.
steps: The committed step of a pathway is usually the regulated one.
For cholesterol it is HMG-CoA → mevalonate.
The enzyme is HMG-CoA reductase.
Statins competitively inhibit it and so lower LDL.

s1-18.ref: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry; Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
w: Correct. OTC deficiency: carbamoyl phosphate accumulates and spills into pyrimidine synthesis, producing orotic acid.
CPS-I deficiency causes hyperammonaemia without orotic aciduria (no carbamoyl phosphate is made).
Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency (citrullinaemia) causes high citrulline.
Arginase deficiency causes high arginine and spastic diplegia, with milder hyperammonaemia.
steps: Hyperammonaemia in a neonate: think urea cycle.
Low citrulline places the block before citrulline: CPS-I or OTC.
Orotic aciduria separates them: present in OTC deficiency.
Male infant fits X-linked OTC deficiency.

w: Correct. Transketolase needs TPP; its activity in RBCs reflects thiamine status.
Erythrocyte glutathione reductase assesses riboflavin (B2).
Erythrocyte aminotransferase assesses pyridoxine (B6).
Pyruvate kinase deficiency is a red cell enzymopathy, not a vitamin test.
steps: Find the enzyme that needs the vitamin as a cofactor.
Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for transketolase.
Measure RBC transketolase with and without added TPP.
A big rise with TPP means thiamine deficiency.

s1-20.ref: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry; Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
w: Correct. HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan) causes purine overproduction, gout and self-mutilation.
ADA deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, not self-mutilation.
Xanthine oxidase deficiency lowers uric acid (xanthinuria), the opposite.
PRPP synthetase overactivity causes gout but not the neurological self-injury picture.
steps: Self-mutilation + gout in a boy = Lesch-Nyhan.
Its enzyme is HGPRT, of the purine salvage pathway.
Without salvage, PRPP builds up and drives de novo synthesis.
Excess purines become uric acid.

w: Correct. Western blot separates proteins and detects them with antibodies.
Southern blot detects DNA.
Northern blot detects RNA.
Lipids are not detected by Western blotting.
steps: Match target molecule to blot name.
Southern was named after Edwin Southern (DNA); the others were named by analogy.
Northern = RNA; Western = protein.
Western blots use antibodies as probes.

s1-22.ref: Harper's Illustrated Biochemistry; Robbins Basic Pathology
w: Correct. Gaucher disease: glucocerebrosidase deficiency, with 'crumpled tissue paper' macrophages.
Sphingomyelinase deficiency (Niemann-Pick) gives foamy cells and a cherry-red spot.
Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs) gives a cherry-red spot without hepatosplenomegaly.
Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency (Fabry) gives angiokeratomas and painful neuropathy.
steps: 'Crumpled tissue paper' cytoplasm is a pathognomonic image clue.
It belongs to Gaucher cells.
Gaucher = glucocerebrosidase deficiency.
Note: enzyme replacement therapy is available.

w: Correct. Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km; Vmax is reached with enough substrate.
Lower Vmax with unchanged Km describes non-competitive inhibition.
Lower Km and Vmax together describe uncompetitive inhibition.
Inhibitors never increase Vmax.
steps: Competitive inhibitor competes with substrate for the same site.
Add lots of substrate and it wins: Vmax is still reached.
But more substrate is needed for half-maximal speed: Km rises.
On a Lineweaver-Burk plot the lines cross on the y-axis (same 1/Vmax).

s1-24.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; Guyton
w: Correct. PGE2 made in the hypothalamus (induced by IL-1, TNF) raises the set point.
Bradykinin causes pain and vasodilation, not fever.
Histamine causes early increased vascular permeability.
Leukotriene B4 is a neutrophil chemoattractant.
steps: Pyrogens act through cytokines (IL-1, TNF).
Cytokines induce COX in the hypothalamus.
The resulting PGE2 resets the thermostat upward.
NSAIDs lower fever by blocking that step.

s1-25.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
w: Correct. Follicular thyroid carcinoma lacks papillary structures and psammoma bodies.
Papillary thyroid carcinoma typically has psammoma bodies.
Serous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary commonly shows psammoma bodies.
Meningioma classically contains psammoma bodies.
steps: Psammoma bodies form in papillary growth patterns.
List the classic four (PSaMMoma).
Follicular carcinoma is follicular, not papillary.
So it is the exception.
s1-25.mn: PSaMMoma: Papillary thyroid, Serous ovary, Meningioma, Mesothelioma.

s1-26.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; Wintrobe's Clinical Hematology
w: Correct. Ankyrin mutations are the most common cause of hereditary spherocytosis.
Glycophorin is not a common cause of HS.
Band 3 is the second most common, not 'only'.
Spectrin (more often beta) is involved in a minority; 'alpha only' is wrong.
steps: HS is a vertical-linkage defect of the RBC membrane.
Several proteins can be involved.
The single commonest is ankyrin.
Spherical cells are trapped and destroyed in the spleen.

s1-27.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; Harrison's
w: Correct. t(15;17) PML-RARA defines acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
CML has t(9;22) BCR-ABL.
Burkitt lymphoma has t(8;14) involving MYC.
Follicular lymphoma has t(14;18) involving BCL2.
steps: Translocation questions are pure recall: build the table.
15;17 = promyelocytic.
It creates PML-RARA, which blocks maturation.
Retinoic acid (ATRA) releases the block.
s1-27.mn: 'APL is 15-17 years old and needs vitamin A (ATRA).'

s1-28.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
w: Correct. Congo red gives apple-green birefringence under polarised light.
PAS stains glycogen and mucins; it is not specific for amyloid.
Prussian blue stains iron (haemosiderin).
Masson trichrome stains collagen.
steps: Amyloid is a protein with β-pleated sheet structure.
Congo red binds it.
Under polarised light it shines apple-green.
Fat pad aspiration is an easy biopsy site.

s1-29.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
w: Correct. Flocculent mitochondrial densities indicate irreversible mitochondrial damage.
Cellular swelling is the earliest, reversible change.
Ribosome detachment from the ER is reversible.
Membrane blebbing is reversible.
steps: Separate reversible from irreversible findings.
Irreversibility = mitochondria cannot recover + membranes are destroyed.
Flocculent (amorphous) densities in mitochondria mark this point.
The other options are early, reversible changes.

s1-30.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease; Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
w: Correct. Minimal change disease shows normal light microscopy and diffuse foot process effacement on EM.
Spike and dome deposits are characteristic of membranous nephropathy.
Wire-loop subendothelial deposits are seen in lupus nephritis class IV.
GBM splitting ('basket-weave') is Alport syndrome.
steps: Nephrotic child = minimal change disease until proven otherwise.
Light microscopy is normal.
Electron microscopy shows effaced podocyte foot processes.
Excellent steroid response.

s1-31.ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease
w: Correct. Classical RS cells are CD15+ and CD30+.
CD20 and CD45 are typically negative on classical RS cells (positive on LP cells of NLPHL for CD20).
CD3 and CD4 are T-cell markers.
CD10 and BCL6 are germinal centre markers (e.g. follicular lymphoma).
steps: RS cells are the malignant cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma.
Their immunophenotype is CD15 and CD30 positive.
They usually lose B-cell markers like CD20.
Popcorn cells of NLPHL flip this pattern.

s1-32.ref: KD Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology; NICE epilepsy guidance
w: Correct. Ethosuximide (T-type Ca2+ channel blocker) is first-line for isolated typical absence.
Carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures.
Phenytoin can worsen absence seizures.
Gabapentin is ineffective and may worsen absences.
steps: 3 Hz spike-and-wave = typical absence.
Absence seizures start in the thalamus via T-type calcium channels.
Ethosuximide blocks these channels.
Avoid sodium-channel drugs, which can worsen absences.

s1-33.ref: KD Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
w: Correct. Protamine, strongly basic, neutralises acidic heparin.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin.
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
FFP replaces clotting factors but does not neutralise heparin.
steps: Heparin is strongly negatively charged.
Protamine is strongly positively charged.
They bind and form an inactive complex.
About 1 mg protamine neutralises ~100 units of heparin.

s1-34.ref: KD Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology; Goodman & Gilman
w: Correct. Phenytoin metabolism saturates near therapeutic levels, so kinetics become zero-order.
Gentamicin follows first-order kinetics (renal excretion).
Digoxin follows first-order kinetics.
Lithium follows first-order kinetics (renal).
steps: First-order: a fixed fraction is eliminated.
Zero-order: enzymes are saturated, so a fixed amount is eliminated.
Phenytoin saturates its enzymes at therapeutic doses.
So small dose changes cause large changes in level.
s1-34.mn: Zero-order drugs: 'PEA' = Phenytoin, Ethanol, Aspirin (high dose).

s1-35.ref: KD Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
w: Correct. Rapid vancomycin infusion releases histamine directly (red man syndrome).
Ceftriaxone can cause biliary sludge and allergy but not this infusion reaction.
Gentamicin causes nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
Metronidazole causes metallic taste and a disulfiram-like reaction.
steps: Flushing of the upper body during an infusion = histamine release.
The classic drug is vancomycin given too fast.
It is not IgE-mediated allergy.
Slow the infusion; antihistamines help.

s1-36.ref: KD Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology; National TB Elimination Programme guidelines
w: Correct. Ethambutol causes dose-related optic neuritis with red-green colour loss.
Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis.
Rifampicin causes orange secretions and enzyme induction.
Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia and hepatotoxicity.
steps: Vision complaint on ATT = ethambutol.
It causes retrobulbar optic neuritis.
Colour vision (red-green) is affected first.
Check vision at baseline and during therapy.

s1-37.ref: KD Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
w: Correct. Amiodarone causes lung fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction, corneal deposits and blue-grey skin.
Sotalol (beta-blocker + class III) causes torsades, not these organ toxicities.
Flecainide (class IC) is proarrhythmic, especially after MI.
Verapamil causes constipation, bradycardia and AV block.
steps: Multi-organ toxicity from one antiarrhythmic = amiodarone.
It is rich in iodine, which explains the thyroid effects.
It is lipophilic, with a very long half-life, so it deposits in tissues.
Monitor thyroid, liver and lung function.
s1-37.mn: Amiodarone checks: 'TLC + eyes + skin' = Thyroid, Liver, Chest X-ray.

s1-38.ref: KD Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
w: Correct. Pralidoxime removes the phosphate group and reactivates acetylcholinesterase.
Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors but does not reactivate the enzyme.
Physostigmine is itself an anticholinesterase; it would worsen poisoning.
Neostigmine is also an anticholinesterase.
steps: OP compounds phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase.
Atropine only blocks the effect at muscarinic receptors.
Oximes pull the phosphate off and restore the enzyme.
This works only before 'ageing' makes the bond permanent.

s1-39.ref: KD Tripathi's Essentials of Medical Pharmacology; ADA Standards of Care
w: Correct. Metformin mainly suppresses hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMPK.
Stimulating insulin secretion describes sulfonylureas.
Alpha-glucosidase inhibition describes acarbose.
SGLT2 inhibition describes gliflozins.
steps: Classify oral antidiabetics by mechanism.
Secretagogues = sulfonylureas; glucosidase = acarbose; SGLT2 = gliflozins.
Metformin is the sensitiser acting on the liver.
Its main effect is reduced gluconeogenesis.

s1-40.ref: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology; Jawetz
w: Correct. Aspergillus: thin septate hyphae with acute-angle dichotomous branching.
Mucor: broad, ribbon-like, pauci-septate hyphae with wide-angle branching.
Candida: budding yeasts with pseudohyphae.
Histoplasma: small intracellular yeasts, not hyphae in tissue.
steps: Note three features: septa, width, branch angle.
Septate + narrow + acute angle = Aspergillus.
Aseptate + broad + right angle = Mucor.
Treatment differs, so the distinction matters.
s1-40.mn: 'Aspergillus is Acute; Mucor is Massive (broad) and at right angles.'

s1-41.ref: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology
w: Correct. India ink shows the thick polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus as a clear halo.
Candida is not capsulated.
Histoplasma is intracellular and not capsulated.
Coccidioides forms spherules, not capsulated yeasts.
steps: CSF + HIV + meningitis: think Cryptococcus.
India ink is a negative stain; the capsule stays unstained as a halo.
Antigen testing is more sensitive than India ink.
Treat with amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole.

s1-42.ref: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology
w: Correct. Group B Strep produces CAMP factor, enhancing S. aureus haemolysis.
S. pyogenes (Group A) is bacitracin-sensitive and PYR-positive.
Enterococcus grows in 6.5% NaCl and bile esculin.
Pneumococcus is optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble.
steps: CAMP = arrowhead haemolysis next to S. aureus.
It is produced by Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B).
GBS colonises the vagina.
It causes neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

s1-43.ref: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology; Harrison's
w: Correct. IgM anti-HBc is positive throughout the window period.
HBsAg has already disappeared during the window period.
Anti-HBs has not yet appeared during the window period.
HBeAg is usually gone by the window period.
steps: Window = gap between HBsAg disappearing and anti-HBs appearing.
Only core antibody bridges this gap.
In acute infection it is the IgM type.
So IgM anti-HBc is the only marker.

s1-44.ref: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology
w: Correct. Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores test autoclaves (moist heat).
Bacillus atrophaeus spores test hot-air ovens and ethylene oxide.
Clostridium tetani is not used as a sterilisation indicator.
Bacillus pumilus tests ionising radiation.
steps: Indicators are the spores most resistant to that method.
Moist heat: G. stearothermophilus.
Dry heat: B. atrophaeus.
Radiation: B. pumilus.

s1-45.ref: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology; Paniker's Parasitology
w: Correct. Crescent (banana-shaped) gametocytes are typical of P. falciparum.
P. vivax gametocytes are round, in enlarged RBCs with Schüffner's dots.
P. malariae shows band forms and rosette schizonts.
P. ovale shows oval, fimbriated RBCs.
steps: Gametocyte shape is the clue.
Crescent or banana = falciparum.
Falciparum smears usually show only rings and gametocytes.
It is the most dangerous species (cerebral malaria).

s1-46.ref: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology; Robbins
w: Correct. Mantoux is delayed-type (Type IV) cell-mediated hypersensitivity.
Type I is immediate, IgE-mediated (anaphylaxis).
Type II involves antibodies against cell-surface antigens.
Type III involves immune complexes (Arthus, serum sickness).
steps: The reaction appears at 48-72 hours, so it is delayed.
